spans.t: This is a small book of ten days, made to go with the Camino de Madrid. In the CaminoPlus catalogue that road runs from Madrid to Sahagún, about 320 km. The app's route notes describe it this way: from the city north over the Sierra de Guadarrama, by way of Segovia, then across the flat Castilian plains to Sahagún, where it joins the Camino Francés. It is a road of about two weeks. Ten days is the length of the reading, not a plan of stages. Read a day twice, or on a rest day, if you like.
Why this book for this road

Teresa of Ávila is a Spanish saint, born in Ávila in 1515: Spain's own saint, and the right companion for a road across its interior. A caution, so that nobody is surprised: the app's route notes for this road name Madrid, the Sierra de Guadarrama, Segovia and the plains to Sahagún, and Ávila is not among them. This book does not claim that the road passes her town. The title names where her story arrives, the small house she founded in Ávila, which you will meet on Day 7.
How a day works
Each day has a morning reading of about five minutes and an evening reflection of about three.
In the morning
there are three parts.

items.t: The passage.
A few lines from Teresa's
Life
, in the exact words of David Lewis's English translation, as printed in 1904. Read the passage twice, the second time aloud if you can. The old English slows the eye, which is half its use.
The reflection.

This part is ours, not Teresa's. It starts from something on the road and lets the passage open it. It says what the passage says, where it is hard, and what it might ask of an ordinary day. It is allowed to doubt.
For the walk.
A question to carry for the next hour and one small practice that needs nothing but attention.

spans.t: In the evening
there are two more.

items.t: At the end of the day.
A look back at the day you have lived, with two or three questions to lie down with.
A short prayer.
Original and brief. If you pray, pray it. If you pray differently, change the words. If you do not pray, say it as a wish, to nobody in particular.

spans.t: A Christian book, and a strange one in places
The
Life

is a Catholic book, written by a Carmelite nun for her confessors in the sixteenth century. It tells of visions, voices and raptures, which she says she cannot always put into words. We chose passages a walker can follow, and where one is strange, the reflection says so calmly. Nothing here asks you to look for such experiences or to copy any penance. Nobody should hurt themselves, or go without food or rest, to read this book well. Teresa herself says that a person who is weak and sickly should not undertake heavy fasting. If you carry a pain you cannot shake, talk to a doctor or to someone you trust. In Spain, 112 is the emergency number.

People walk for many reasons: faith, sport, grief, curiosity, a rest from work. All are welcome here. You do not need to believe what Teresa believed to recognise a woman who was tired of herself, who asked for help, who was laughed at, and who started again.
The shape of the ten days
The days follow the shape of her life, and also the shape of a walk.

Day 2

Day 3

Day 4

Day 5

Day 6

Day 7

Day 8

Day 9

Day 10

spans.t: These are a shape, not a timetable. If you are tired, read the passage and the prayer and leave the rest.
On the road and at home

Read the morning part on a bench, in a bunk, in a café while the soup arrives. Then put the phone away and take the question with you for an hour. Read the evening part last of all, when the boots are off. At home it works the same way: the morning with your tea, the evening before bed.
Three words you will meet.
Albergue
is the simple hostel where pilgrims sleep, often in bunks. The
credencial
is the pilgrim's passport, stamped along the way.
Buen Camino
is what walkers say to one another on the road, roughly, may your Way go well.

chapters.title: About the book and its author

spans.t: The woman

Teresa was born in Ávila on 28 March 1515. The translator's preface says that in the world, and even as a nun, she was known as Doña Teresa Sanchez Cepeda Davila y Ahumada. She entered the Carmelite monastery of the Incarnation in Ávila as a young woman. The edition's notes disagree about the year, so we give none.

In 1562 she helped begin a small, very poor and strict house in Ávila, the monastery of St. Joseph, and the preface dates the start of the Reform of the Carmelites to its opening on 24 August that year. A censor who examined her book in 1575 believed she had founded a dozen monasteries in the previous thirteen years. She died in 1582. The Church honours her as a saint, and the edition's title calls her St. Teresa of Jesus.
The book
The
Life

is the story of her soul, "Written by Herself", as the title page says. In her Prologue she says that she had been "commanded" to describe her way of prayer, and she writes "this account of myself which my confessors command me to give". She addresses one confessor as "my father" again and again. According to the translator's preface, a Dominican friar, Pedro Ibañez, ordered her to put the story of her spiritual life in writing. She began in the monastery of the Incarnation and finished a first account in Toledo in June 1562. The preface supposes that this account ended at the thirty-first chapter, and that the later chapters were added when another Dominican told her to write the history of the new foundation.

The edition has forty chapters and a Prologue: childhood and struggle first, then her teaching on prayer from the eleventh chapter, then visions, the founding in Ávila, and four last chapters of further graces.

Her contemporaries were careful about it. A respected spiritual master, Juan of Ávila, read it in 1568 and wrote that its teaching on prayer was for the most part sound, and that it should not be put in everybody's hands. The Inquisition kept a copy for years, and Teresa never saw it again. A Dominican, Domingo Bañes, who examined it for the Inquisition, wrote in 1575 that he found nothing erroneous in its doctrine. He doubted the visions, but not her goodness. It was first printed after her death, in Salamanca in 1588, edited by Fray Luis de León. The original, in her own hand, is kept at the Escorial.
Why it suits a pilgrim
The
Life

is written from the middle of things. Teresa is ill, tired, doubtful, short of time and opposed, and still going. She describes the days when she did not want to go in, the day something stopped her, the people who held out a hand, and a plan that everyone told her to drop. It is also unexpectedly funny: she laughs at herself, at her singing, at her excuses. For a walker who is bored on the third day or discouraged on the eighth, that is useful company.
What is hard, and what we left out

She is very hard on herself, and calls herself wicked on page after page. Where it comes up, we say what she says about it herself: that a humility which torments is not the true kind. The visions and raptures are in the book, and we have left nearly all of them aside. The
Life

also holds a vision of hell and some frightening accounts of the devil, which we have not used. It speaks of Protestants in the language of a sixteenth-century Catholic, and we have left those places out. And it describes a way of life with fasts and penances that this book does not recommend to anyone.
The translation, the edition and the licence

The English in the passages is by David Lewis, who, according to the edition's introduction, was born on 12 November 1814 and died on 23 January 1895. His translation was first printed in 1870, with a second edition in 1888. We use the third edition, enlarged, published in London by Thomas Baker and in New York by Benziger Brothers in 1904. It carries a re-imprimatur, the Church's permission to print, dated 27 September 1904 and signed Franciscus, Archbishop of Westminster. Its introduction and notes are by Fr. Benedict Zimmerman, a Carmelite, who says the translation was made from Don Vicente de la Fuente's Spanish edition of 1861 and 1862. Lewis and Teresa are long dead, so the translation is in the public domain. It is on Project Gutenberg as ebook number 8120, and every quotation here was checked against that text, word for word.
What we changed in the passages is nothing. We kept the old spellings and forms, such as
Thou
and
Thy

. The edition numbers its chapters with Roman numerals, as the attributions do, and numbers its paragraphs; we left out the paragraph numbers and the footnote numbers. Where a passage skips a stretch, a mark like this shows it: …. We quote only Teresa's own words, never the introduction, the translator's preface, the annals or the notes, though some facts on this page come from them.
The choice and order of the passages, the reflections, the questions and the prayers are ours, and original. Nothing of the Project Gutenberg licence text or trademark is copied here.
Who put the first stones of your road in place?
The passage

paras.t: I had a father and mother, who were devout and feared God. Our Lord also helped me with His grace. All this would have been enough to make me good, if I had not been so wicked. My father was very much given to the reading of good books; and so he had them in Spanish, that his children might read them. These books, with my mother's carefulness to make us say our prayers, and to bring us up devout to our Lady and to certain Saints, began to make me think seriously when I was, I believe, six or seven years old. It helped me, too, that I never saw my father and mother respect anything but goodness. … As soon as I saw it was impossible to go to any place where people would put me to death for the sake of God, my brother and I set about becoming hermits; and in an orchard belonging to the house we contrived, as well as we could, to build hermitages, by piling up small stones one on the other, which fell down immediately; and so it came to pass that we found no means of accomplishing our wish.

cite.t: The Life of St. Teresa of Jesus

spans.t: Reflection

If you leave from Madrid, the first hour is streets: crossings, kerbs, a city still waking up. The app's route notes call it a city start, and after that the road turns toward the Sierra de Guadarrama. Wherever your own first hour is, one thing holds for it. You did not invent this road, or the boots, or the idea of walking so far. Someone lent you a map, or told you a story, or left a book on a shelf. The walk began before you did.

Teresa starts her Life in the same place, with the people who set her going. She was born in Ávila in 1515, and her book opens on a house. The picture is plain. Her father liked good books and kept them in Spanish so that the children could read them. Her mother made sure they said their prayers. Nothing in it is grand. What Teresa picks out is what the children saw: that she never saw her father and mother "respect anything but goodness".

The same shelf, as she says in her next chapter, held another kind of book too. Her mother was fond of tales of chivalry, and the children read them, taking care that their father never saw. A house can set you going in two directions at once, and the good one is not always the louder.

Then comes the part that makes people smile, or wince. Between the two halves of the passage, she tells how she and the brother nearest her in age read the lives of the saints together. When they read of martyrs, it struck her that the vision of God was "very cheaply purchased". So they planned to go to the country of the Moors, "begging our way for the love of God", and be beheaded there. Their difficulty, she says, was their father and mother. An editor's note in this edition, drawing on an early biographer, adds that the two had crossed the bridge outside the city gate before an uncle met them and brought them home.

Take that plan calmly. It is a child's plan, and a dark one: two children hoping to be killed for God. Teresa does not praise it. Looking back, she says it was "not out of any love of Him of which I was conscious". She wanted to arrive quickly. Nobody should read this and wish for martyrdom, and nobody should copy any severity from these pages. What you can take is smaller and sunnier: a child who read about a road and wanted to walk it.

When that failed, the children did something they could manage. They built hermitages in the orchard from small stones, "which fell down immediately". It is hard to think of a better first picture for a long walk than a tower of loose stones that will not stand. Stone on stone, and down it comes. Teresa does not say they tried again. She does say the wish stayed. A few lines later she writes that she contrived to be alone "for the sake of saying my prayers", and that there were many of them.

There is a harder thing in the passage, and it is better said at once. On her first page Teresa says that a good home "would have been enough to make me good, if I had not been so wicked". She will say something like this again and again, and it can wear on a reader. She was writing for confessors who had told her to describe her prayer. In her prologue she says she would have liked to speak of her sins in detail, and was held back. Yet the faults of her girlhood that she actually names are a taste for books of chivalry, fussing over her hair, and gossip with cousins. She is hard on herself. You do not have to agree with every verdict to keep reading, and in a few days she will say something about that habit herself.

What does it ask of an ordinary morning? Mostly to look back before you look forward. On the first day of a long walk the mind runs ahead to the end, to Sahagún, to the bed tonight. Teresa's own first page is about the beginning: the shelf, the bedtime prayers, the brother, the orchard, the stones that would not stay up. It suggests that your road also began with small things, set in place by people who may not know that you are here.
For the walk

items.t: Who set the first stones of this walk in place: the one who lent a rucksack, who told the story, who is waiting at the other end?

For the first ten minutes, count your steps in tens. At each ten, name one person who is behind this walk, and let that be the whole thought. If you run out of names, begin again with the first. If a name brings something sore with it, keep it company for one step more, then go on to the next.

spans.t: At the end of the day

The first evening of a walk has a taste of its own. The legs report in, one by one. The pack comes off and the body seems to float for a minute. Whatever the day was, it is behind you, and a long road is ahead of you. That is a good moment for the people who set you going. They are mostly absent now, and they are easiest to think about when you are sitting down.

Teresa's mother comes back into the Life a little later in the same chapter. She died young. Teresa says that her mother was only thirty-three, and that she herself was about twelve, a little less. In her grief she went to an image of Our Lady, and, in her words, "with many tears implored her to be my mother". Reading that, you may think of your own loss, or of nobody in particular. Some people walk for a reason of that kind, and many walk for no such reason. Either way the evening can make room. If you carry someone, you can set them down beside the bed for the night. They will still be there in the morning.

It is worth remembering that not everyone had a house like hers. The passage is not a reproach. Teresa counts three sisters and nine brothers, a noisy house, and she says she was "the most cherished of my father", which did not make her path easier. If your own first house was cold or thin, the road still began somewhere. Some people set out because of where they came from, and some in spite of it. Both are walking.

Think also of the stones. Most days, something goes up and something falls down. A plan for the afternoon that was too ambitious. A conversation that did not build into anything. A resolve about pace, made at breakfast and abandoned by eleven. The children in the orchard could not make a wall that stood. They gave up that plan and kept the wish behind it. If today's plan changed (the distance, the bed, the hour you left), look at what lies underneath. You wanted to walk, and you walked. That may be enough to call the day well spent. It is no great comfort to be told so, and it is some comfort to be shown it, in a book written more than four centuries ago.
Before you sleep, lay out tomorrow's clothes, fill the bottle, and put the boots where you can find them in the dark. These are small stones, set the night before, and they stay up.

On the first night the body is not sure what has been asked of it, and it may take a few days to settle. Sleep comes before any big thought. If this evening's questions feel heavy, answer one and leave the other.

items.t: Who set me on this road, and have I thanked them?
What did I try to build today that would not stand, and can it wait until tomorrow?
What did I long for as a child that I could still try, in a smaller form?

spans.t: A short prayer

Thank you for those who set me going. For the shelf of books, the bedtime voice, the hand on the shoulder at the door. Let what I build today be small enough to stand. Where something fell, let me begin again in the morning. Keep close the ones I carry, and let me sleep.
What do you do on the days when you do not want to go in?
The passage

paras.t: When I was in the midst of the pleasures of the world, the remembrance of what I owed to God made me sad; and when I was praying to God, my worldly affections disturbed me. This is so painful a struggle, that I know not how I could have borne it for a month, let alone for so many years. … And certainly the violence with which Satan assailed me was so irresistible, or my evil habits were so strong, that I did not betake myself to prayer; and the sadness I felt on entering the oratory was so great, that it required all the courage I had to force myself in. They say of me that my courage is not slight, and it is known that God has given me a courage beyond that of a woman; but I have made a bad use of it. In the end, our Lord came to my help; and then, when I had done this violence to myself, I found greater peace and joy than I sometimes had when I had a desire to pray.

cite.t: The Life of St. Teresa of Jesus

spans.t: Reflection

There is a moment, early on a hard morning, when you take the phone out to see how far you have come. Four kilometres. It felt like forty minutes of nothing. You put it away, and six minutes later you take it out again. Soon the walking is mostly the looking, and the road is something to be got through. You may know that kind of hour. Perhaps it comes after a bad night, or on a flat stretch where nothing changes, or on the third day, when the novelty has worn off and the end is not yet near.

Teresa knew a version of it that lasted years. She was a nun, and a person of prayer by habit, and she says she spent nearly twenty years "on this stormy sea, falling and rising, but rising to no good purpose". Her chapter has a picture of it that every walker can read. For some years, she says, she was "more occupied with the wish to see the end of the time I had appointed for myself to spend in prayer, and in watching the hour-glass", than with anything else. She sat there to be finished.

The passage names the cause of the trouble, and it is a divided heart. When she was among the pleasures of the world, she remembered what she owed to God and was sad. When she knelt to pray, her worldly affections disturbed her. So she had neither. Later in the chapter she puts it in a short line: she had "no sweetness in God, and no pleasure in the world". Whatever you make of her particular pleasures, the shape is familiar. It is the state of being at the desk and wanting the beach, and then on the beach thinking about the desk. She says she does not know how she bore it for a month, "let alone for so many years".

In the lines just before, she says what she means by courage. She knows of nothing "which requires greater courage than plotting treason against the King, knowing that He knows it, and yet never withdrawing from His presence". It is a stern picture, and the point of it is the staying. She came to prayer with her divided heart in her hands and did not hide it or leave.

What interests her is what she did. The sadness she felt on entering the oratory was so great, she says, that it took all her courage "to force myself in". That is the whole story of the courage. It is not a heroic act. She walked through a door, again, on a day when she did not want to. She adds, with a flash of dry humour, that people say her courage is "not slight", and that she has made a bad use of it.

Then comes the line that gives the passage its weight. When she had done this violence to herself, she says, she "found greater peace and joy than I sometimes had when I had a desire to pray". The days of forcing herself in were worth more than the days of wanting to. A word on "violence": as Teresa uses it here, it means a push against her own reluctance, a hand on the door. There is no fasting in this passage, and no hurting of the body, and it would be a misreading to look for any.

Be honest about the limits. She gives her trouble two names within one sentence: the violence with which Satan assailed her, or her own strong habits. A modern reader may add others: guilt, tiredness, a mind pulled two ways. Her body was often ill in those years, as her sixth and seventh chapters say plainly. And not every reluctance deserves to be overruled. A sharp pain in a knee, or dizziness in the heat, is the body telling you to stop, and listening to it is not weakness. The courage she means is for the ordinary dread of beginning, the one that sits at the door, not for the warning that comes from the foot.

So what is asked of you? Probably something small: go in. Do the first ten minutes before you decide anything. The hour-glass will go on running whether you watch it or not, and a watched one is slow. You may find that the stretch you most dreaded is the one you can hardly remember at the end of the day. Teresa claims no more than that, and no less. She says she did not go in because she wanted to. She went in, and afterwards she was glad.
For the walk

items.t: Is this reluctance telling me something I should heed, or is it only asking me to start?

For the first ten minutes, put the phone away and keep no count of distance or time. Walk by feel. At the end of the ten, ask yourself whether you still want to stop. If the answer is yes because something hurts, stop, and look after it.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Somewhere in the day you probably looked at the clock more than you would like to admit. It is the oldest habit of the road. How far now, how long to the next village, how many hours until the bed. There is nothing wicked in it. The only question worth asking is what it did to you. Did it help you pace yourself, or did it empty the hour of everything but the number?

Think back to the doors you did not want to go through. The first step out of the room this morning. The long afternoon stretch. The café you were tempted to sit in until the day was over. At each of them you either went in or did not. Teresa makes no claim that going in always feels good. She says only that the peace she found when she forced herself was sometimes greater than the peace she found on the days she wished to pray. Whether that held for you today, only you know. If you did go in, on a day with no glow in it at all, give that a quiet nod. Nobody stamps a pilgrim's passport for it.

A day measured in kilometres looks different when you remember it as a day. The numbers are in the app. The day itself is somewhere else: a smell, a dog behind a gate, a bench, a stranger's good morning. Try to find three things from today that have no number attached. They are usually still there when the figures have faded.

An honest word about tiredness. In the evening the body argues for skipping everything, and a small practice can feel like one demand too many. Keep this one small. A reflection that takes two minutes and is done lying down is a reflection. If you have to choose, choose sleep over thought, and let the questions wait for the morning.

Dread of tomorrow's start can arrive in the evening too. The sadness Teresa describes came before she reached the door of the oratory. If the first hour of tomorrow is already heavy in your mind, notice that it is the picture of the hour that is heavy. The hour itself is ten minutes of walking.

There is one more thing in Teresa's account that deserves a quiet nod. She says she could not have borne the split life for a month, and she bore it for years. Nobody should ask that of themselves, and this book does not. It asks for the next ten minutes. If a longer heaviness has settled on you, one that does not lift with rest and a good meal, it is worth saying so to a doctor or to someone who knows you. On the road in Spain, 112 is the number to call in an emergency.

items.t: When did I most want today to be over, and what was I doing then?
What did I begin today that I did not feel like beginning?
Was there a moment when stopping was the wise thing, and did I listen?

spans.t: A short prayer

Be with me at the doors I do not want to enter. Give me the first ten minutes of tomorrow, and I will find the rest. Where I am pulled two ways, make me whole enough to walk. Where I am only tired, let rest be answer enough.

chapters.title: Day 3. The picture in the corner

spans.t: What finally makes you stop?
The passage

paras.t: My soul was now grown weary; and the miserable habits it had contracted would not suffer it to rest, though it was desirous of doing so. It came to pass one day, when I went into the oratory, that I saw a picture which they had put by there, and which had been procured for a certain feast observed in the house. It was a representation of Christ most grievously wounded; and so devotional, that the very sight of it, when I saw it, moved me--so well did it show forth that which He suffered for us. So keenly did I feel the evil return I had made for those wounds, that I thought my heart was breaking. I threw myself on the ground beside it, my tears flowing plenteously, and implored Him to strengthen me once for all, so that I might never offend Him any more. … But this last time, before that picture of which I am speaking, I seem to have made greater progress; for I was now very distrustful of myself, placing all my confidence in God. It seems to me that I said to Him then that I would not rise up till He granted my petition. I do certainly believe that this was of great service to me, because I have grown better ever since.

cite.t: The Life of St. Teresa of Jesus

spans.t: Reflection

Some days a thing you have passed a hundred times stops you. A wall, a tree, an old man's wave from a doorway. Nothing about it has changed. What has changed is you, and the reason is usually tiredness. A rested walker walks past. Someone who has been going on for days, and is tired of the sound of their own thoughts, may find the road has given them a wall to lean on.

Teresa's turn came like that. Her ninth chapter begins with six plain words: "My soul was now grown weary." She had been a nun for about twenty years. The annals printed with this edition set the scene in 1555, when she was about forty. She had been praying and not praying, going in and drifting out, and the habits she had picked up "would not suffer it to rest". Then, one day, she went into the oratory and saw a picture that had been put there for a feast. It was an ordinary object. Someone had set it in a corner.

What she saw was Christ badly wounded, and the picture, she says, was so well made that it moved her. She felt how poorly she had repaid those wounds, and thought her heart would break. She threw herself on the ground beside it and begged to be strengthened "once for all".

This is a Christian picture, and the book says so. The guilt in it is heavy, and phrases such as "the evil return I had made" may jar if you do not share her faith or her way of speaking about herself. Notice, though, what the picture does. It does not lecture. It ends the bargaining. For years she had been trying to arrange a life that kept both prayer and pleasure, and in front of this image she could not keep the arrangement up. If you do not pray, you may know a version of it: a photograph, a letter, a stretch of road that strips away the excuses for a minute.

Look at the second half of the passage. She says "this last time", and the words matter. There had been earlier tears, earlier resolutions; earlier in the same chapter she describes placing herself in thought at Christ's feet, after the example of the Magdalene, in the hope that her tears would not be despised. So this was not the single moment of a story. It was one of a series, the one that held. What was different? She says she was "very distrustful of myself, placing all my confidence in God". The earlier turns had been her own efforts. This time she stopped relying on them.

And she was stubborn. She seems to remember telling Him that she would not rise until her petition was granted. It is a child's kind of prayer, and an old woman's. You may not pray at all, and still recognise the posture: sitting down in the road and refusing to go further until something is settled.
A little later in the chapter she is given Augustine's
Confessions

. She writes: "I thought I saw myself there described." What troubled her was that Augustine and the other saints she loved had been called once, and had stayed called, while her own relapses were "now so many". She took courage again, she says, from remembering how much she was loved: "Of His mercy I never doubted once, but I did very often of myself."

Be careful not to make the turn bigger than she does. She does not say she was cured. She says "I have grown better ever since", which is modest, and the chapters that follow still hold fear, doubt and long dry spells. A turn is where a road bends, and the road goes on. The morning after it is usually plain. The picture is in its corner, the boots are where you left them, and the first hour has to be walked like any other.

In practice it comes to letting yourself be stopped, which is harder than it sounds on a walk that is mostly about going on. And it comes to being wary of the plan that rests on your own strength alone. Whatever help you reach for, a friend, a doctor, a prayer, a bench, Teresa's report is that the turn came when she stopped trying to manage it by herself.
For the walk

items.t: What would stop me today, if I let it?

When something catches your eye on the way, a view, a door, a picture in a church, stop for one full minute. Do not move on until the minute is over. Let the thing be what it is, and notice what it asks of you, if anything. If nothing catches your eye in the first hour, choose something plain and give it the minute anyway: a gatepost, a puddle, the line of the next hill.

spans.t: At the end of the day

You have probably stopped today, whether you meant to or not: at a crossing, at a fountain, at a bar for coffee, at a bench when the legs said so. Most stops on a long walk are practical. A few are something else. The difference is hard to explain, and easy to notice afterwards. A stop that was practical leaves you ready to go. A stop of the other kind leaves you slightly changed.

Teresa has a gentle note on this in the same chapter. She says it helped her "to look on fields, water, and flowers", and that the sight of these things "was as a book unto me". They woke her up and brought her back to herself. If you were outdoors today, you may have had a little of that without looking for it: a ditch with water in it, a field, a flower you could not name. The evening is a good time to bring one of them back.

She mentions a small habit from the same years. For a long time, "nearly every night before I fell asleep", she thought for a little while about one scene, and it became as fixed as the sign of the cross before sleep. A turn needs something small like that to keep it from fading, a few lines at the end of the day that do not depend on how you feel. It might be a name, a view, a line of a song. It does not have to be a prayer.

Look, too, at the way she asks. She does not make a vow in front of the picture. She begs to be strengthened, so that she may never fall again. That is a request, and a vow is a promise. It matters at the end of a long day, when it is easy to promise the moon: tomorrow you will walk slower, eat better, call home, stop being short with the person in the next bunk. A request is gentler, and more honest about what you can do alone. It leaves room for the help that may come.

The turn she describes is not a thing to wait for tonight. You may be tired of something in yourself: a habit, a mood, a way of talking to people you love. You do not have to settle it before you sleep. It is enough to admit it, once, to yourself. Teresa put it off for years, and she is plain about the cost.

The body at the end of a long day is a poor judge of its own life. A decision made on a bunk at nine o'clock is often wrong by breakfast. So do not decide anything big tonight. Note only what stopped you, and what you are tired of, and let the rest sleep. And if nothing stopped you today, that is a day too. Some stretches of road simply go by. The picture was in its corner for the feast, and nobody knows for how long before she looked at it.

items.t: What stopped me today, even for a moment?
What am I tired of in myself, and have I said so to anyone?
Where did I let a field, a stream or a flower say something to me?

spans.t: A short prayer

Let me be stopped by what matters. Where I have been going in circles, let me sit down. I cannot mend myself by trying harder. Hold what I cannot hold, and give me rest tonight, and a clear head in the morning.

chapters.title: Day 4. Four ways to water a garden

spans.t: Which kind of water is this morning asking for?
The passage

paras.t: A beginner must look upon himself as making a garden, wherein our Lord may take His delight, but in a soil unfruitful, and abounding in weeds. His Majesty roots up the weeds, and has to plant good herbs. … Let us now see how this garden is to be watered, that we may understand what we have to do: how much trouble it will cost us, whether the gain be greater than the trouble, or how long a time it will take us. It seems to me that the garden may be watered in four ways: by water taken out of a well, which is very laborious; or with water raised by means of an engine and buckets, drawn by a windlass--I have drawn it this way sometimes--it is a less troublesome way than the first, and gives more water; or by a stream or brook, whereby the garden is watered in a much better way--for the soil is more thoroughly saturated, and there is no necessity to water it so often, and the labour of the gardener is much less; or by showers of rain, when our Lord Himself waters it, without labour on our part--and this way is incomparably better than all the others of which I have spoken.

cite.t: The Life of St. Teresa of Jesus

spans.t: Reflection

Where the summers are dry, whoever keeps a garden thinks about water before anything else. You may pass a vegetable plot on the way, a stone trough beside it and a hose coiled on a nail, and see at once that the plot is a daily argument with the sky. There are only so many ways to get water to a plant. They differ mostly in how much of the work is yours.

Teresa chose a garden for her best-known picture of prayer. She says she is not sure where she found it: "I have either read or heard of this comparison; but as my memory is bad, I know not where". She also apologises for using it at all, "because I am a woman, and write simply what I have been commanded". She is writing for a confessor, on his orders, and she expects him to smile: "your reverence will be amused when you see my stupidity". The humour is part of the picture. She is not laying down doctrine. She is reaching for whatever will make the matter plain.

Here are her four waters, plainly. First, water drawn from a well by hand, which is laborious. Second, water raised by a wheel and buckets turned with a windlass, less work and more water. She adds that she has "drawn it this way sometimes", so she knew what it was to turn that handle. Third, a stream or brook running to the garden, which soaks the soil and leaves the gardener far less to do. Fourth, rain, "when our Lord Himself waters it, without labour on our part".

She then applies them to what she calls four degrees of prayer. The well is where everyone begins, when you must work to gather yourself, and the effort is great because the mind has been used to wandering. The three that follow are, in her account, increasingly a matter of gift. And here the book changes. The chapters on the three higher waters describe states of absorption that she says came to her unasked, and her language grows strange. She calls one of them "a glorious folly, a heavenly madness". Again and again she says she cannot find the words. We have not quoted those chapters, and we do not pretend to explain them.

It is worth knowing how she herself handled them. She warns against trying to force them: "it is of great moment not to raise our spirit ourselves, if our Lord does not raise it for us". Her own contemporaries examined such experiences with care, and she wanted them examined. Nothing in this book asks you to look for anything of that kind. The most ordinary part of the picture is the most useful: the well, and the person turning the handle.

Then there is a reading of our own, which is ours and not hers. On a walking day you may know all four waters. The well is the plain work: the first hour, the pack, the blister you tape. The wheel is whatever eases the work, a good rhythm, a pole, the right socks. The stream is the stretch where the walking walks you, and you hardly notice the kilometres go. The rain is what you could not arrange: a view at a bend, a kindness from a stranger, a morning that is simply good. You cannot order any of the last two. You can keep the garden ready for them.

On an ordinary day this comes to three things. First, be honest about which water you have. A day at the well is not a failed day. Teresa says "the labour is greatest at first", which is true of the first day of a walk and the first week of anything. Second, do not despise the work. She tells the gardener to do what lies in his power and leave the rest, even when the well is dry. We will come back to that on Day 9. Third, be ready for rain without waiting for it. A gardener who sits indoors until it rains has a poor garden. A gardener who is out in the beds when it comes has a good one.

If you do not pray, try reading "garden" as attention, the thing you tend, and "Lord" as whatever you call the part of life that you did not make. The picture still holds. The work is yours. The weather is not.
For the walk

items.t: Which of the four waters is this morning: the well, the wheel, the stream or the rain?

Wherever you see water on the way, a trough, a ditch, a tap, stop to drink and name which of the four your day is at the moment. Do not try to change it. Only name it, and go on. If there is no water in sight, drink from your own bottle. The exercise is the naming, not the place.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Which water was today? Most days are a mixture. The morning at the well, the afternoon on the wheel, ten minutes of stream, and perhaps one unasked drop of rain. It helps to be exact about it, because the mind likes to flatten a day into good or bad. A day with one drop of rain is not a bad day, and a day at the well all the way is not a wasted one.

Teresa has a sentence to hold on to when the comparisons begin. One of the men who had told her to write, she says, had been raised in four months to a greater height than she had reached in seventeen years. Her advice, to herself and to anyone: "Close the eyes of your imagination, and do not ask why He gives devotion to this person in so short a time, and none to me after so many years." Walkers know that temptation well. Someone passes you who seems to float, or you hear of a person who walked twice your distance and cried at the end. It is easy to feel behind. The road does not keep a league table, and neither does the garden.

She also says something about weeds. The beginner, in her picture, is making a garden in poor soil full of them, and she says that His Majesty "roots up the weeds". The gardener's task is to water. It is a relief to read it that way. You are not required to pull up every fault in yourself by nightfall. Some of it is not yours to do. Keep the buckets going and let the rest be.

Her garden is also not for the gardener alone. It is made "wherein our Lord may take His delight", not for the one with the bucket. If you do not pray, you can still ask who your day's attention might refresh. A greeting at a gate is water for someone else's garden, and it costs a breath.

Notice, too, how little she asks for. She hopes the water will be given "drop by drop", and she says that when she drew "but one drop of water out of this blessed well", she considered it a mercy. A garden lives on drops. It may help to count yours: one real conversation, ten quiet minutes, a meal eaten slowly with nothing else going on. None of them will look like much in a diary. They are what the roots take up.
A long day at the well takes it out of the arms. If today was all work and no rain, let tonight be rest. A dry well is not a fault in the gardener. It may only be a hot week.

items.t: Which water did I draw today, and which came without my drawing it?
Whom did I compare myself with, and what did it cost me?
What did I try to do today that was not mine to do?

spans.t: A short prayer

Let me do the watering that is mine. Let me not demand the rain. Where the well was dry, keep the roots alive. Where something came that I did not earn, let me say thank you and not hold it too tight. Water the garden tonight while I sleep.
Who is walking beside you, and have you said thank you?
The passage

paras.t: It is a great evil for a soul to be alone in the midst of such great dangers; it seems to me that if I had had any one with whom I could have spoken of all this, it might have helped me not to fall. I might, at least, have been ashamed before him--and yet I was not ashamed before God. … For this reason, I would advise those who give themselves to prayer, particularly at first, to form friendships; and converse familiarly, with others who are doing the same thing. It is a matter of the last importance, even if it lead only to helping one another by prayer: how much more, seeing that it has led to much greater gain! … I had many friends to help me to fall; but as to rising again, I was so much left to myself, that I wonder now I was not always on the ground. I praise God for His mercy; for it was He only Who stretched out His hand to me.

cite.t: The Life of St. Teresa of Jesus

spans.t: Reflection

Some of the best minutes of a walking day happen off the road. A table where somebody passes the bread. A bench where two strangers compare feet. On a busy way you may share a long table every evening. On a quiet one, a nod across a counter may be the whole of the company. Either is enough to change an afternoon, and it is odd how little it takes.

Teresa has spent six chapters on her youth, her illness and her first falls, and in the seventh she stops to say what would have helped. It is not a technique. It is a person. She says it is a great evil for a soul to be alone in the midst of such great dangers, and that if she had had anyone to talk to, it might have kept her from falling. Then she adds a reason that is not at all grand: "I might, at least, have been ashamed before him". She says she was not ashamed before God. She was, though, perfectly capable of being ashamed before a friend.

There is honesty in that. Part of what a friend is for, she suggests, is that you cannot easily pretend in front of them. A secret kept in your own head can be argued into almost any shape. Said aloud to someone who has walked a similar way, it shrinks or it hardens, and either is useful.

Her advice follows at once: "form friendships", and talk freely with others who are doing the same thing, even if it comes to no more than helping one another by prayer. You can see how practical it is. She does not say find a master or join a society. She says find someone on the same road, and speak plainly.

Then comes the line that makes her smile ruefully. She had "many friends to help me to fall", she says, but for rising again she was "so much left to myself" that she wonders now she was not always on the ground. It is a good warning against a lazy reading of her own advice. Not every friendly person is a friend in her sense. Earlier in this same chapter she tells of long conversations with visitors that wasted her years, and says she was fond of the person who distracted her most. The question is which way a friend leans you when they lean.

She is also careful to point to the people who did help. In her third chapter it is a nun who slept in the same room and talked to her about God: "How well she used to speak of God!" It is an uncle, whose books she read aloud to him, though she did not like them much at the time. It is a Dominican confessor, who "took upon himself the task of helping my soul in earnest". None of them is a hero. They do the dull, reliable thing of paying attention.

The passage ends in thanks. "I praise God for His mercy", she says, "for it was He only Who stretched out His hand to me". You may read the hand in two ways. If you pray, it is God's. If you do not, it may be the hand of the person who happened to be there, or a stranger on a road who passed on the right word. Teresa goes one way, and you may be glad of her gratitude without going with her. What stays true either way is that the hand is held out, and you take it.

Gratitude is almost a habit of breathing in her book. After many hard admissions she writes "May He be blessed for ever!" and goes on. In her last chapter she records a worry she had: whether it showed a lack of detachment to enjoy the company of the people who looked after her soul. The reply she wrote down is this: "It is not a virtue in a sick man to abstain from thanking and loving the physician who seems to restore him to health when he is in danger of death." She says those words were spoken to her in prayer. However you take that, the sentence is sound by itself. It is not noble to refuse help, or to be too proud to say thank you.

Three small things follow from all this. Accept the help that is offered, the shared plaster, the direction, the seat. Thank people exactly, by naming what they did. And, if you are carrying something heavy, let one person know. This does not forbid solitude. Teresa loved it and sought it, as she says more than once. It says only that the heaviest things are not meant to be carried alone.
For the walk

items.t: Who has helped me up this week, and have I thanked them in words?

Say one thank-you today that is exact. Not "thanks for everything" but "thank you for holding the gate", or "thank you for the water". If you meet no one to say it to, write the message and send it tonight. If it is hard to find the words, begin with the plain fact of what the person did and let the rest follow.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Think through the day for hands. Not the large ones. The woman at the counter who found you a seat. The walker who pointed out the arrow you had missed. The friend at the other end of a message who answered at once. A good deal of kindness goes by in a day without being counted, because most of it is small enough to fit into a single sentence.

Then think about the other kind of company. Some talk at the table lifts everyone, and some talk pulls everyone down. You may have joined in a round of complaints about the road, or the beds, or other walkers, and felt lighter for a moment and heavier afterwards. Teresa's phrase about friends who help you fall was not a joke only at her own expense. It asks you to notice which evening conversations were good for you and which only used up the time. A simple test is whether you stood a little straighter when it ended.

The hand goes both ways. In the same seventh chapter Teresa is the one who helps. She had given her father books about prayer and talked with him about it, and he made such progress, she says, that she praised God for it. When he fell ill, she says, "I went to nurse him", though she was ill herself. A friend is not only someone who steadies you. Think whether you steadied anyone today: held a door, shared the last of the water, listened a minute longer than you wanted to.

Being a good companion at the end of a long day can be one more job. You are allowed to go to bed early. You are allowed to say that you are going to rest, and to leave the table kindly. A friend who sleeps well is better company tomorrow than one who stays up to be nice.

If you walk alone, tonight may feel quiet in a way that stings. Quiet is not an accusation. A friend need not be in the room. A message, a memory, or a person you plan to see at the end can be company enough for an evening. Teresa's whole book is a long letter to a man who was somewhere else, whom she addresses as "my father", the way one speaks to a priest. Company can travel by page.

Before you sleep, try a small practice that asks for no writing. Name three people from today, not three blessings, three people, and say thank you to each of them in your head, one sentence apiece. If it is only the person who sold you the bread, that is fine. It is easy to thank a day in general, and gratitude in general is thin. Gratitude with a face is not.

items.t: Who held out a hand to me today, and did I see it at the time?
Whose company left me lighter, and whose left me heavier?
Whom could I thank tomorrow morning, by name and for something exact?

spans.t: A short prayer

Thank you for the hands held out to me today, the ones I saw and the ones I missed. Give me good company on the road, and the sense to be good company. Where I am alone tonight, let me be alone gently. Where someone needs a word from me in the morning, wake me in time.
What would change if you said plainly what you do not know?
The passage

paras.t: One of my faults was this: I had a very imperfect knowledge of my Breviary and of my duties in choir, simply because I was careless and given to vanities; and I knew the other novices could have taught me. But I never asked them, that they might not know how little I knew. … My singing of the Office was bad, and I felt it much if I had not learned the part intrusted to me,--not because I made mistakes before our Lord, which would have been a virtue, but because I made them before the many nuns who heard me. I was so full of my own reputation, that I was disturbed, and therefore did not sing what I had to sing even so well as I might have done. Afterwards, I ventured, when I did not know it very well, to say so. At first, I felt it very much; but afterwards I found pleasure in doing it. So, when I began to be indifferent about its being known that I could not sing well, it gave me no pain at all, and I sang much better.

cite.t: The Life of St. Teresa of Jesus

spans.t: Reflection

You come to a junction with no arrow. The phone says one thing and the ground another. A boy is walking a dog along the lane. You can go on and hope, or you can ask. Asking costs a moment of looking like someone who does not know the way, and that moment can feel surprisingly expensive.

Teresa paid that price in advance. In this passage the thing she does not know is small: the Breviary, the book of daily prayers, and her part in the Office, the set of prayers the sisters sang together in choir. Other novices could have taught her. She says so. But she "never asked them", she writes, "that they might not know how little I knew". It is hard to read that without a small laugh of recognition. The thing she was protecting was her reputation, and it was a flimsy thing.

Then she lets us watch what the protection cost. Her singing was bad, she says, and she felt it. The worst of it was where the pain came from. It was not that she made mistakes in front of God, "which would have been a virtue", but that she made them in front of the other nuns. She was "so full of my own reputation" that she was disturbed, and so she sang worse than she might have. Fear of being found out took her breath and her pitch.

And then the turn, which is the funniest and most hopeful part. She began to say, when she did not know a part well, that she did not. At first it hurt. Then she found pleasure in it. When she grew indifferent to people knowing she could not sing well, it gave her no pain at all, "and I sang much better". In a sentence just before the stretch we have quoted, she says that now, "even when I know a thing, but yet am very slightly in doubt about it, I ask the children". She has lost nothing by it, she says, "neither honour nor credit". She suspects her memory improved.

Humility, in this account, is not self-contempt. It is saying what is so: I know this, I do not know that, I need a hand with the other. The young novices she asked had a small and useful gift, and she was glad of it. The fear had been about status, and it spoiled the singing.

This matters because Teresa herself, elsewhere in her book, can sound as if humility meant calling herself wicked on every page. She offers a test for telling the real thing from the other. In her thirtieth chapter she says that "true humility is not attended with trouble; it does not disturb the soul; it causes neither obscurity nor aridity: on the contrary, it consoles". Of a false one, which pictures the worst and leaves the soul in the dark, she says it gives "no light for any good work". In the same chapter as our passage she looks back at a fear of being praised and says "I understood afterwards that this was not true humility, because it disturbed me so much". So when she is hard on herself, you may remember that she warned against exactly that, and you do not have to join in.

There is one more small picture in this chapter, which is a different sort of humility altogether. She used to fold up the sisters' mantles as they left the choir, secretly, thinking of herself as serving the angels who had been there praising God. When the sisters found out she was ashamed. The shame came, she says, not because she was humble but because she was afraid they would laugh. Her virtue, she says, "was not strong enough to bear that they should know of it". Even the secret kindness had her vanity in it, and she says so cheerfully.

For a day on the road, then: ask the question. Say "I am lost" and "I can't manage the last four kilometres" and "I don't know what that bird is", plainly, to the person next to you. And hold the other side loosely too. There is no prize for being the most self-effacing walker on the road. If you are praised, say thank you and be done. If you are wrong, say so and carry on. Most of what looks like humility is truthfulness. Most of what is hard about it is the first moment.
For the walk

items.t: Where am I pretending today to know something I do not?

Ask one real question of someone you meet: the way, the name of a plant, how their day has been. Mean it, and listen to the answer. Or do one small service that nobody will see, and let it stay unseen. Pick it up from the road: a bottle in the verge, a loose stone moved off the path, a word of encouragement to the walker behind you. Then walk on without telling anyone.

spans.t: At the end of the day

At the end of a day there is a small ledger that has nothing to do with kilometres. It records the times you smoothed something over. Said "fine" when you were not fine. Nodded as if you knew what was being said. Took the credit for a good guess. These are very small lies, and they cost about what Teresa's cost her, which is some of your breath.

She is a good guide to this, because she does not stop at the shame. Later in the same chapter she catches herself doing the opposite. When she saw that someone thought well of her, she would find some roundabout way to let them know of her sins, "that seemed to relieve me". Her confessor told her to stop. She decided it was not humility at all but "the result of temptation". In the next paragraph she says, with an edge: "I was therefore not humble, but a coward." It is worth remembering at the end of a day when you have been busily putting yourself down. Playing small can be a way of hiding. It protects you from being asked for more.

Notice, too, whom she asked. She says she asks "the children", the youngest and least regarded of the house. There is a lesson in the choice. We tend to ask the person who looks as if they know: the one with the guidebook, the one in the good boots. Often the person who knows is the one who lives here, the child on the corner, the old woman at the window. Think whether today you asked the right sort of person, or only the sort who would not make you feel small.

So the truth runs between two errors: the show of knowing and the show of not knowing. Your day probably had some of each. You may have bluffed at breakfast and played yourself down at supper. Nothing needs to be settled tonight. Just see which of the two you lean towards, and how it feels in the body, because the body usually knows first.

There is a small thing to try over supper, if there is a supper. Ask the person beside you a question to which you do not know the answer, and mean it: where the day began for them, what they carry, what they are walking toward. You may find that the wish to look as if you knew things was a weight you had not noticed carrying all day.

Fatigue is a great breeder of small untruths, since it is easier to say "fine" than to explain. If you can say one true thing tonight to the person nearest you, "I am done in", you will have done a day's work in humility. The rest can wait for rest.

items.t: Where did I pretend today to know the way?
What small service did I do that I would not mind being unseen?
Where did I play myself down to avoid being asked for more?

spans.t: A short prayer

Let me say what I know, and no more. Let me say what I do not know, and not be afraid. Keep me from the show of knowing and from the show of modesty. Let the small things I did today be enough, seen or unseen. Let me rest in what is true.

chapters.title: Day 7. This house is not mine

spans.t: What do you do when the long thing stays long?
The passage

paras.t: Now and then everything seemed to fail; particularly one day, before the Provincial came, when the prioress ordered me to meddle no more with it, and to give it up altogether. I betook myself to God, and said, "O Lord, this house is not mine; it was founded for Thee; and now that there is no one to take up the cause, do Thou protect it." I now felt myself in peace, and as free from anxiety as if the whole world were on my side in the matter; and at once I looked upon it as safe. … Writing thus briefly, it is impossible for me to explain what took place during the two years that passed between the beginning and the completion of the monastery: the last six months and the first six months were the most painful. … In this way they came to approve of what they had condemned; and so, by degrees, they withdrew from the lawsuit, and would say that they now felt it to be a work of God, since His Majesty had been pleased to carry it on in the face of so much opposition.

cite.t: The Life of St. Teresa of Jesus

spans.t: Reflection

Every long walk has a middle. The start is behind you, with its nerves and its fresh socks. The end is out of sight. What is left is a long run of days that look much alike. The app's route notes describe the last part of this road as flat stages across the Castilian plains, and a flat stage has its own kind of trial: nothing to climb, nothing to conquer, only the same field and the same sky and the road going on.

Teresa's passage comes from the middle of the longest trouble in her book. She wanted to found a small house of nuns in Ávila, very poor and very strict, and nearly everyone told her not to. Her own monastery disliked the idea. In her words, people said it was folly. The Provincial, who had approved, changed his mind. Later, the town authorities met and resolved to break the new house up, and a lawsuit began. She had no money, she says, and no idea what to do. When she looks back she says that she cannot explain what happened in the two years between the beginning and the completion, except this: "the last six months and the first six months were the most painful".

Hold on to that last phrase. You may recognise it from a walk of your own. The hardest stretches of a long task are often the very beginning and the very end. The beginning is hard because nothing has yet shown that it will work. The end is hard because you are tired and it is not quite over. The middle may be long and dull, and still easier on the spirit than either.

The moment she describes in the first part of the passage is the lowest. Everything seemed to fail. The prioress, her superior, ordered her to meddle no more and to give it up altogether. Teresa went to God, as she says, and spoke to Him plainly: this house is not mine, it was founded for You, and since nobody is left to take up the cause, You protect it. What follows is the part to notice. She felt peace "as if the whole world were on my side in the matter", and at once she looked upon it as safe.

Read that as a walker. Nothing outside had changed. The prioress had not relented, the lawsuit was still running, the money had not arrived. The change was in her hands, which had been clenched around the whole thing and now were open. She did not stop working. A few lines before our passage she writes that the servants of God inside the house "did more by their prayers than I did with all my negotiations, though the affair needed the utmost attention". Both statements stand: the matter needed attention, and she could not carry the outcome. She did her part, and she handed back the rest.

There is a doubt that belongs here, and it should be said. Letting go can be a polite name for giving up. How would you tell? Teresa's answer is in her habits rather than her feelings. She went on taking advice, and she was prepared to be told she was wrong. She says that if wise men had found a fault in the whole matter, she "would have given up the founding of a thousand monasteries". She also admits, at the height of the opposition, that she "thought that people were partly in the right". She was not a woman who thought she could not be mistaken.

Then the end, in the last stretch of our passage. The people who had resisted the new house came round. They "came to approve of what they had condemned", she writes, and in time they "withdrew from the lawsuit". Hear this as one woman's report, told by the person for whom it worked. A road does not always end that way. Many hard things are abandoned, and some of them rightly. Her story is not a promise. It is an example of someone who kept working at the thing that was hers, took good advice, and let go of the thing that was not.

One last caution, since the house she founded lived under a strict rule. Nobody should read this day as a call to hard fasting or to any harshness toward the body. The stubbornness in the passage is for a project, in the open, with advisers. It is not an ordeal chosen for its own sake.

Put plainly, the middle of a road asks for this. Do your part for the hour you are in. Let the finish be someone else's business for today. And when the road is long and flat and the same, let the sameness be what it is, a kind of weather that passes.
For the walk

items.t: What am I carrying today that is not mine to carry?

At the next bench, post or bend in the road, name one worry you cannot act on before tonight. Say, silently, "not mine, for now", and leave it there. Do the same again at the next landmark, with whatever you have picked up in between. By the end of the stage the pack may feel lighter, though it holds exactly what it held.

spans.t: At the end of the day

The middle of a long walk has a particular tiredness. It is not the first-day soreness or the last-day eagerness. It is a flat, steady wear, the feeling of being a long way from both ends. If that is where you are tonight, do not take it as a sign that something is wrong. It is what a middle feels like.

Think back to what in today was yours to do. The legs, the feet, the water, the pace, the greeting, the decision about where to sleep. Those were yours, and you did them. Think, then, about what you carried that was not yours: next week's problem at home, a message that cannot be answered until tomorrow, a worry about something miles away. You may have carried it all day, and it weighed the same as a stone in the pack.

Teresa has one more detail worth keeping, from three chapters earlier. When the first plan collapsed and her confessor told her to drop it, she did. She says she remained quiet "for five or six months, neither thinking nor speaking of the matter". It would be easy to pass over that, but it is an act of discipline, and rarer than starting. She did not nag it, or revive it every morning. She waited, and she says she never lost the sense that it would be done. You may have something that wants that kind of waiting, a decision, a hope, a conversation. Tonight is not the time to push it.

One more thing from the same chapter, for evenings. On the day the house was founded, Teresa says, she was so happy she was beside herself. About three or four hours afterwards a crowd of doubts came down on her: had she done a foolish thing, would the nuns bear the rule, what business was it of hers? She says her anguish was "like one in the agony of death", and "one of the most distressing moments I ever passed in all my life". Then it lifted. She puts it down to the devil. You may put it down to being tired and keyed up, after a day that asked a lot. Either way, she draws the lesson that "No joy is lasting; everything is liable to change". If the evening brings doubts about the whole walk, they may be the tail of the day and not a verdict on it.

There is also the other side of persistence, which is stopping. Some tiredness is not weather, it is a message. A foot that hurts more each day is information. So is a cold, or heat that has left you dizzy. If a rest day would help, take it, and do not think of it as failing. A person you trust, or a doctor, can tell you better than the road can. Teresa's persistence was a wise person's persistence, with advisers beside it.

items.t: What did I do today that was mine to do, and did I do it?
What did I carry that was never mine?
Whom could I ask whether to press on or to rest?

spans.t: A short prayer

Let me do my part and hand back the rest. Where the road is long, give me a pace I can keep. If I am told to stop, let me hear it kindly. What is not mine to carry, let me put down tonight, and let me sleep.

chapters.title: Day 8. A little bird with weak wings

spans.t: How large a hope are you allowed to carry, and how small a step does it need?
The passage

paras.t: We must have great confidence; because it is very necessary for us not to contract our desires, but put our trust in God; for, if we do violence to ourselves by little and little, we shall, though not at once, reach that height which many Saints by His grace have reached. … His Majesty seeks and loves courageous souls; but they must be humble in their ways, and have no confidence in themselves. I never saw one of those lag behind on the road; and never a cowardly soul, though aided by humility, make that progress in many years which the former makes in a few. I am astonished at the great things done on this road by encouraging oneself to undertake great things, though we may not have the strength for them at once; the soul takes a flight upwards and ascends high, though, like a little bird whose wings are weak, it grows weary and rests.

cite.t: The Life of St. Teresa of Jesus

spans.t: Reflection

Some mornings start with a hill that looks too big at breakfast. If you cross the Sierra de Guadarrama, the app's route notes mention the Navacerrada pass on the way into the province of Segovia, and that is the sort of morning where you look at the line on the map and say nothing. A simple question arrives. Is this too much? There are two ways of answering it wrongly, and Teresa's chapter has something to say about both.

The first wrong answer is the timid one, dressed as modesty. In the same chapter she warns that the devil hinders those who start to pray by giving them a false notion of humility. "He makes them think it is pride to have large desires, to wish to imitate the Saints, and to long for martyrdom." She calls this a trick. A person is told that it would be presumptuous to hope for much, and the hope is quietly put away. Any walker who has said "I'm not the sort of person who does this" has been given the same line. It sounds humble. It is mostly fear.

Against it she sets the passage. We must have "great confidence", she says, and not shrink our desires, but put our trust in God. We will reach, "though not at once", the height that many saints have reached. Then comes her line about courage: God "seeks and loves courageous souls; but they must be humble in their ways, and have no confidence in themselves". Notice the two halves. Courage and humility are not opposites. The courage is to want a great deal. The humility is to know the wanting does not rest on your own strength. A walker has a version of this: you decide to cross the mountain, and you also know that you need water, a forecast, and a good start.

She then gives a picture that suits tired people better than any slogan. The soul "takes a flight upwards and ascends high", she writes, "though, like a little bird whose wings are weak, it grows weary and rests". The bird rests. It does not come down in disgrace. Resting is part of the flight, and the weak wings are not hidden. In the sentence before she says that great things are done by "encouraging oneself to undertake great things, though we may not have the strength for them at once". The word to keep is "at once". Nothing here asks for a leap. It asks for a direction, and for the long business of getting there a bit at a time.

Her chapter has fences around all this, and they matter. A little earlier in it she writes "Discretion is necessary throughout". Further on, in the same teaching, she says it would be wrong for a person who is weak and sickly "to undertake much fasting and sharp penances", or "any austerities of this kind". She means it. She does not want large desires turned into harm to the body. She also has a sharp joke against advisers who are too cautious: she does not want a director who would "teach us to crawl like toads", nor one who is satisfied when the soul "shows itself fit only to catch lizards". Courage with discretion, then. And the passage's own phrase, "do violence to ourselves by little and little", belongs with those fences. As she uses it here, it means the steady effort of choosing the harder good thing a little at a time. It does not mean harshness.

She leans for support on three short remembered lines. One is from Paul: that all things are possible in God. Another is Augustine's prayer: "Give me, O Lord, what Thou commandest, and command what Thou wilt." The third is a picture: "St. Peter lost nothing by throwing himself into the sea, though he was afterwards afraid". Notice that last clause. Peter was afraid afterwards, and still lost nothing. Courage is not the absence of fear. It is moving while afraid, and Teresa gives herself that permission.

Be straight about the risk. Large hopes can lead to bad decisions on a mountain. Weather can change, and a pass in cloud is not a pass in sun. Start early, carry more water than you think you need, look at the forecast, and be ready to turn round without shame. 112 is the number for emergencies in Spain. Courage here includes the courage to stop. The same Teresa who says "not at once" would say it to you.

Day to day, then, name the large hope, perhaps only to yourself. Then reduce it to the next step you can see: the next bend, the next tree. Rest as the bird rests. And when someone, perhaps your own voice, says that it is pride to hope for much, ask whether it sounds more like humility or like fear.
For the walk

items.t: What large thing am I allowed to hope for from this walk, and what is the next small step toward it?

On the first climb of the day, pick a tree, a corner or a post a little way ahead. Walk to it, breathe, look back at how far you have come, then pick the next. If the weather turns or the air is hot, shorten the steps rather than the plan.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Think of what you dared today. It need not have been a mountain. It may have been a conversation with a stranger in halting Spanish, or walking a kilometre further than you meant to, or deciding to stop when you wanted to push on. Courage has no fixed size. It is measured by how far it took you from what was easy.

Teresa has one more sentence for the evening, from her thirty-first chapter. She says it is very necessary for our weak nature that we have great confidence, and that we should not suppose "if we do our best" that we shall fail "to obtain the victory at last". It is a kind sentence, because it is conditional. It does not say you will win. It says that doing your best is not a doomed thing, and that you need not walk as though it were.

A hard day shows courage and caution as friends. By evening the day's decisions are visible: where you started early, where you took the longer way round, where you turned back. If one of them looked like a retreat, set it beside the bird. Nothing in Teresa's passage says the wings must carry the bird the whole way in one go, and nobody asked it to.

The evening also shows the sentences you said to yourself. "I am not the sort of person who does this." It might have been about hills, or Spanish, or asking for a room, or sleeping in a dormitory. The voice that says it is quiet and sounds sensible, which is just how Teresa describes the false humility that makes people shrink their wishes. Today's walk may have contradicted it somewhere. If you can find the place, keep it. It is evidence.

The bird with weak wings rests. How did you rest today? Resting is easy to do badly: sitting on a wall and scrolling, or lying on a bunk in a knot of worry. A real rest has a loosening in it. If you had one, however brief, give it credit. If you had none, make a small one now, with your feet up and your hands open.

If you want a large hope for tomorrow, name it in a single sentence tonight and leave it on the pillow. Hopes are better kept in a rested head, but a sentence put down now will still be there at breakfast, and you will not have to find it again.

After a day of daring, the evening can bring the thing Peter felt afterwards. The fear arrives once the danger is behind you. Your knees may shake in the bunk when they did not on the path. That is not weakness returning. It is the body catching up with what it did.

items.t: What did I dare today, and what did it cost me?
Where did I rest like the bird, and did I let myself?
Where did I say "I am not the sort of person who..." today, and was it true?

spans.t: A short prayer

Give me a large hope and a small step. Let me trust the ground and the plan, and know when to turn back. Where my wings are weak, let me rest and not call it failure. Carry me a little, as far as the next bend.

chapters.title: Day 9. The well with no water

spans.t: What do you do on the days when nothing comes?
The passage

paras.t: God grant there may be water in it! That, however, does not depend on us; we are drawing it, and doing what we can towards watering the flowers. So good is God, that when, for reasons known to His Majesty--perhaps for our greater good--it is His will the well should be dry, He Himself preserves the flowers without water--we, like good gardeners, doing what lies in our power--and makes our virtues grow. … What, then, will he do here who sees that, for many days, he is conscious only of aridity, disgust, dislike, and so great an unwillingness to go to the well for water, that he would give it up altogether, if he did not remember that he has to please and serve the Lord of the garden; if he did not trust that his service was not in vain, and did not hope for some gain by a labour so great as that of lowering the bucket into the well so often, and drawing it up without water in it? It will happen that he is often unable to move his arms for that purpose, or to have one good thought: working with the understanding is drawing water out of the well.

cite.t: The Life of St. Teresa of Jesus

spans.t: Reflection

Some days have no weather in them and no view. The sky is the colour of the road. The legs are working, the feet are fine, and still nothing arrives: no pleasure, no sense of meaning, only the next step and the one after. If you are on the flat stages that the app's route notes describe, such a day may come in the second week, when the plain stretches out and the early excitement has gone. Nobody has done anything wrong. The well is simply dry.

You met Teresa's well on Day 4. This is the same garden on a worse morning. Here the gardener comes to the well and lowers the bucket and draws it up empty, and does it again. She says what this feels like in a list that reads like a doctor's note: "aridity, disgust, dislike, and so great an unwillingness to go to the well for water". He would give the whole thing up, she says, if he did not remember that he serves the Lord of the garden, and trust that his service is not in vain. And on some of those days, she says, he cannot even move his arms for the work, or have one good thought.

The passage opens with the line that frees the gardener: "God grant there may be water in it! That, however, does not depend on us." We are drawing it, and doing what we can. When God, for reasons of His own, wills the well to be dry, He "preserves the flowers without water". That is a generous idea. The flowers do not die on the day the water fails. The roots have more in them than the gardener can see.

Her advice in the next lines is a little sweeter than most of us can swallow. She asks the gardener to take comfort in the trust that has been shown him. It is the greatest favour, she says, to labour in the garden of so great an Emperor, to be trusted with the work when no reward shows. Some readers will take to that and others will not. If it does not help you, leave it. Her second thought is plainer: it is not the feeling that counts. She says "the love of God does not consist in tears, nor in this sweetness and tenderness which we for the most part desire". A person who is "determined not to care much, neither to rejoice nor to be greatly afflicted, whether sweetness and tenderness fail it, or our Lord grants them", she says, "has already travelled a great part of the road".
