You can read that as trust in a different form: the walk counts whether or not it feels like anything.

Then comes the part many modern readers will be glad of. A few paragraphs on, she takes up the question of why the dry times come, and she is practical to a degree that surprises. She says dryness "comes most frequently from bodily indisposition". The changes of the seasons and the humours of the body, she writes, can compel the soul "without fault of its own, not to do what it would, but rather to suffer in every way", and "this poor prisoner of a soul shares in the miseries of the body". Her advice follows. Do not force it: the more we force the soul on these occasions, "the greater the mischief, and the longer it lasts". "The poor soul must not be stifled." Make a change in the hour of prayer. "Take care, then, of the body." Rest, eat, and let there be recreations, such as conversation, or "going out into the fields". The soul, she says, should not be dragged but carried gently.

You are already on that prescription. A walker goes out into the fields every day. So when the day is dry, her advice is first of all domestic. Eat properly. Drink. Take your shoes off at the stop. Sit with someone, or sit alone, and look at the fields. Do not hold yourself responsible for a mood that may only be a hot week, a poor night, a blister, or an empty stomach. And do not turn dryness into a verdict on the whole walk.

Be honest about the limit. If the dryness goes on for weeks and takes the colour out of everything, that is a matter to take to a doctor or to someone you trust, and not to a garden image. Teresa herself says more than once that a person who suffers in this way needs a guide with experience, and she sought one out again and again. A long flat spell is a reason to ask someone, not to endure alone.

The whole of it, for a dry day, is to lower the bucket anyway. It is to do the plain, near, next thing and not demand that it taste of anything, and to look after the body as though it were a friend who is also tired.
For the walk

items.t: What is one small, plain thing I can do for the garden today, whether or not I feel anything?

Lower the bucket: do one small thing as well as you can without asking how it feels. Fill the bottle. Tape the heel. Say good morning and mean it. Then, at the next stop, take her advice and look after the body: sit down properly, eat something, drink, and let your eyes rest on a field.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Dry days are the ones that do not make it into stories. Nothing happened. You walked, you ate, you slept, and the whole day went by with the sound turned down. If today was one of them, give it a nod. It is the commonest kind of day on any long road, and the kind that does the most to make the rest possible.

Teresa has an image for it in another chapter that may help. She writes about a person who has often travelled a certain road and who, "though it be night and dark", knows by that experience "where he may stumble", because "he has seen the place by day". On dry days the feet are doing what the days of light have taught them. You did not feel like it, and you walked, because you had walked before. Your habits carried you, and that is not a lesser thing than inspiration. It is what inspiration leaves behind.

She has one more suggestion for the days when the main thing will not come. There are "exterior works, as of charity", she says, that can be done instead, though at times the soul will not manage even those. In plain terms: when you cannot feel, you can still do. Buy the bread for the person beside you. Hold the door. Carry something for someone who is struggling. A kindness done on a dry day has the same weight as one done on a good day, and it often has the added benefit of getting you out of your own head.

One thing to be careful about is the verdict you pass tonight. A tired mind in a quiet room is a harsh judge. It may tell you that the whole walk is pointless, or that you are a person who cannot feel anything, or that the thing you hoped for from this road is not coming. Teresa's reply, in effect, is that you are being asked to judge a day on one bucket. The garden is bigger than the bucket, and the weather will move.

Dryness is also lonelier when it is hidden. A sentence said aloud, "this was a flat day", to whoever is near, often loosens it. You do not need a remedy from them. You may find that they know the feeling too. And if nobody is near, say it to the page, to a message, or to the dark. It stops being a secret, and that is half of its weight.

Dry days and tired days are close cousins, and a good night's sleep clears some of the dryness for no reason anyone can name. If you can, go to bed a little earlier than usual. If you cannot sleep, do not argue with the dark. Lie on your back and listen to the building for a minute.

items.t: What did I do today without feeling it, and what did that teach my feet?
What did my body ask for today, and did I give it?
Whom could I tell, simply, that today was dry?

spans.t: A short prayer

Be with me when the well is dry. Let me lower the bucket anyway, and not ask for a drop. Teach me to look after this body as a friend. Keep the flowers alive tonight without water, and let me not be ashamed of a plain, empty day.
What goes home with you, and what does an ordinary Tuesday need?
The passage

paras.t: We are not angels, for we have a body; to seek to make ourselves angels while we are on the earth, and so much on the earth as I was, is an act of folly. In general, our thoughts must have something to rest on, though the soul may go forth out of itself now and then, or it may be very often so full of God as to be in need of no created thing by the help of which it may recollect itself. But this is not so common a case; for when we have many things to do, when we are persecuted and in trouble, when we cannot have much rest, and when we have our seasons of dryness, Christ is our best Friend; for we regard Him as Man, and behold Him faint and in trouble, and He is our Companion; and when we shall have accustomed ourselves in this way, it is very easy to find Him near us, although there will be occasions from time to time when we can do neither the one nor the other.

cite.t: The Life of St. Teresa of Jesus

spans.t: Reflection

There comes a day, a few days after a walk, when the rucksack is emptied onto a bedroom floor. The shirts smell of the road. The boots stand by the door looking puzzled. The kettle is the same kettle, and the post has piled up. If your walk ends at Sahagún, where this road joins the Camino Francés, or goes on beyond it, or if you are only reading this at your own table, the question is the same. Where does all of it go now?

Teresa's answer, in this passage, is one of the plainest things in her book. "We are not angels, for we have a body." She says it in a chapter that answers certain books on prayer, written by people she respects. Those books advised the advanced to put away every image and every human support. Teresa says that this seems right enough now and then, but that to withdraw altogether is more than she can endure. She also tells how she tried the advice herself and came to think it a mistake for her, adding at once, "still, it may be that it is I who am deluded". To try to make ourselves angels while we are on the earth, "and so much on the earth as I was", she says, is an act of folly. It is a small joke at her own expense, from a woman who was often ill, often tired and always busy.

"In general, our thoughts must have something to rest on." Think of what that means to someone who has been walking. A bench. A shell on a rucksack. A route you know in your legs. A cup of coffee at a certain bar. These are not distractions from the pilgrimage. They are the things that held it up. And coming home is a matter of finding the new benches: the chair by the window, the walk to the shops, the usual hour.

Then comes her list, which is as good a short account of an ordinary life as any: "when we have many things to do, when we are persecuted and in trouble, when we cannot have much rest, and when we have our seasons of dryness". Busy, pressed, short of sleep, and dry. That is a Tuesday. It is also, in a way, the whole of this book, since you have met every item on the list. In such times, she says, "Christ is our best Friend", for we see Him as a man, "faint and in trouble", and He is our companion. This is a Christian sentence and says so. Its sense for a reader outside the faith is still clear: you do not have to be at your best to be accompanied. A companion who knows what it is to be tired and in trouble is better than a lofty one.

There is a gentle rebuke in the lines around the passage, aimed at anyone who comes back from a pilgrimage wanting the holy life without the washing-up. In the same chapter she warns against "seeking to be Mary before it has laboured with Martha". The reference is to the two sisters in the Gospel, one of whom sat and listened while the other got on with the meal. Teresa's point is that the work of the house is not the enemy of the inner life. It is where you begin. You may not be ready for the quiet, and the dishes may be the proper start.

She is also honest about how much of her own life was spent in the middle of things. Near the end of the book she writes, "I have so little time", and says that writing the account was a trouble. She hopes it will prove "a blessed trouble" if it does some good. The book you have been reading was made in the gaps of a busy life, by someone with little time to spare. That seems the right note on which to end a pilgrimage: not arrival at a summit, but a return to work with something added.

And the book does not end on a summit. In the last chapter she records words that were said to her, she says, to console her: that "in this life we could not continue in the same state". She says she was told to expect it to be like this: "At one time I should be fervent, at another not; now disquieted, and again at peace, and tempted; but I must hope in Him, and fear not." You can hear these as spoken from outside or as the conclusion of a shrewd woman looking back over her life. In either case they remove a pressure. You may not be able to hold on to the best day of the walk, and nothing says you should. What you can keep is smaller and more durable.

What goes home with you is mostly small and bodily. Unpack. Wash the clothes. Eat at a table. Call the people who have wondered. Then pick one habit from the road that will fit into a kitchen, and put it where you will see it.
For the walk

items.t: What from this road will I carry into an ordinary Tuesday?

Choose one habit from the walk that fits in a house: ten quiet minutes at the start of the day, a short walk after supper, one exact thank-you every evening. Say it aloud once. Then do it tomorrow at the usual hour, for a week, before deciding anything else. If it is hard to keep, make it smaller until it is easy, and then keep that.

spans.t: At the end of the day

If this is your last evening on the road, or the first at home, it can feel odd. The days had a shape, and the shape is about to go. The body that learned to rise early and walk will wake up tomorrow with nowhere to go. You may find the quiet louder than you expected.

Look back over the ten days of this book, as you would look back down a road from a rise. A house with a shelf of books and stones that fell down. An hour-glass watched. A picture in a corner. Four waters. A hand held out. A question put to a child. A lawsuit and a handing back. A small bird that rests. A well with no water. And now a body, and a kettle. There is a road in it. It is not a road to a mountain top. It is the road of a person who kept on going in, who kept on asking, who set her hand to the work in front of her, and who wrote it down in the spare hours.

Soon someone will ask, "How was it?" and the easy answer is "fine". Have one true sentence ready instead, small enough to say at a door or over a coffee. Not the whole walk. One picture: the plains in the evening, a stranger's bread, the day the well was dry. Teresa's whole book is that kind of act, a person telling a few trusted listeners what happened and what it was like, as plainly as she could. A true sentence is a gift to the one who asked.

Teresa does not promise that the best of it can be kept. The words she records are that we do not stay in one state. That can be read as a weariness, or as a mercy. After a good walk, the mind wants to hold the good. A gentler wish is to carry its manner, the early start, the patience, the habit of saying thank you, and let the feeling come and go as the weather does.

A last small thing for the evening is to mark the end of the walk, however quietly. Wash the boots. Put the shell, the credencial or the ticket where you will find it. Say thank you, to somebody or to nobody, for ten days of a road and a book. Endings need a little ceremony, even a kitchen-sized one, or they leave the day open.

The body often catches up after the walk is over. It may be heavier for a day or two than it was on the road. Rest is not a betrayal of the pilgrimage. It is a part of it. And if a long low mood follows the end of the walk, one that does not lift after some days of ordinary life, talk to a doctor or someone you trust.

items.t: What do I most want to carry from this road into an ordinary week?
Who needs to hear that I am home, or that I am grateful?
What small, plain thing will I do tomorrow at the usual hour?

spans.t: A short prayer

Thank you for the road, for its long middle and its dry afternoons. Let me carry home something small enough to fit in a kitchen. Give me the plain tasks, and the grace to do them well. Be with me on ordinary days as you were on the road. Let me rest, and let me begin again.

You have come to the end of the ten days, or you are stopping early, or you plan to go back to a day you skipped. Any of these is fine. The book is not a course, and nobody is marking it. It was made to be a little company on a road across Spain, and company does not have to stay once the road is done.
Ten small things
Ten small things fit in a pocket, and each is something you have already held once.

items.t: The stones that would not stand, and the wish that stayed.
The hour-glass: going in anyway, for ten minutes, on a day with no wish to.
The picture in the corner, and being stopped by it.
The four waters: the work that is yours, and being ready for rain.
The hand held out, and a thank-you that is exact.
The children, and asking plainly.
The house that is not mine: doing your part and handing back the rest.
The little bird with weak wings: a large hope, a small step, a rest.
The well with no water: lowering the bucket, and looking after the body.
The body and the kettle: we are not angels.

spans.t: Pick one. Choose the one you can remember without looking. It will do more for you than all ten kept in a drawer.
Going on

If you would like more of Teresa, she is easy to find. The edition we have used is on Project Gutenberg as ebook number 8120, and it is the same text every passage here was checked against. Our ten days come from chapters I, VII, VIII, IX, XI, XIII, XXII, XXXI and XXXVI. The edition also prints, after the
Life
, a set of shorter papers by Teresa called the Relations, and before it a long introduction by its editor, which you can skip.

A warning is fair. Much of the book is about visions, voices and raptures that we have left aside, and a good deal of it is about her sins, which she describes in a way that may seem extreme. Read on if you want to, and read what helps. Pass quietly over what does not. Teresa herself, in this book, was careful about the strange parts, and asked wise people to judge them.

Some of it will not have worked, and that is fair too. A day that left you cold on the road may speak to you at your own table in March. A passage that asked for more belief than you had was not a test you failed. If something hardly touched you, put it down. Nothing has gone wrong.
A last word

Teresa does not end her book on a summit. She ends it with a request that her reader be careful with it, with the news that she had little time to write it, and with a hope that she and he may one day see more clearly the mercies they have been shown. It is an ordinary ending, a letter coming to a close, and it is more believable for that.

If you keep only one thing, keep the sentence from her last chapter that tells you what you may expect: that in this life we do not continue in the same state. Some days fervent, some not, some quiet, some troubled. The advice that goes with it is short: hope, and do not be afraid.
Walk again when you can. Or tomorrow, ten minutes after supper, to the end of the street and back, with one bucket and no particular rain in mind.
Buen Camino.
